figures.caption: Figure 1: SCRIBE constructs interpretable, context-aware semantic features that are used to predict brain activity, enabling the modeling of the dynamic nature of meaning in the brain. It combines three information sources: a cognitively grounded semantic feature space (Binder et al., 2016), a target concept, and the linguistic context in which the concept appears. For each semantic property in the feature space, LLMs are prompted independently to assign a score reflecting how strongly the property applies to the concept in context. These property-wise scores are then aggregated across models to produce the final representations, which are used as input to a brain encoding model that predicts fMRI responses.

Table 2: Human contextual judgments and their alignment with the SCRIBE ensemble. (a) Mean semantic feature scores for human judgments (computed from all ratings) and SCRIBE across the low-target (LT), original (O), and high-target (HT) conditions, with one-sided Wilcoxon signedrank tests over concept–property pairs for the predicted directional contrasts. (b) Human reliability and human–SCRIBE alignment in each condition. ICC(1, 8): reliability of the mean of 8 participants; ceiling = √ ICC(1, 8), the maximum correlation attainable given human noise. r: Pearson correlation between SCRIBE and the mean human rating; r/ceiling: correlation normalized by the noise ceiling, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over concept–property pairs. MSE: mean squared error between SCRIBE and the mean human rating, with the chance level obtained by shuffling SCRIBE scores across pairs (1000 permutations) in parentheses. Values are averaged over 20 balanced subsamples of 8 ratings per item, as required for comparable reliability estimates across items. All ICCs, correlations and MSEs are significant (p ≤ .001, permutation tests).

Figure 2: (a) Voxel-wise differences in brain alignment between contextual and out-of-context variants of SCRIBE (SCRIBEC − SCRIBEO) for a representative subject (subject 3). Red regions show higher predictive accuracy for the contextual model. Improvements due to contextualization are predominantly observed in language-related cortical regions. (b) Brain alignment for SCRIBEO, QAEmb, and SCRIBEC across the whole brain and language-related ROIs. Bars represent mean performance across subjects, with individual subject values overlaid and error bars indicating the standard error. Red asterisks (∗) denote statistically significant differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Contextual SCRIBE (SCRIBEC) consistently outperforms its out-of-context (SCRIBEO) variant, while achieving performance comparable to QAEmb.

Figure 3: Unique neural variance explained by SCRIBEC and QAEmb. (a) Spatial distribution of voxel-wise unique variance for a representative subject (subject 2). Red indicates greater unique variance explained by SCRIBEC, whereas blue indicates greater unique variance explained by QAEmb. (b) Region-wise comparison of uniquely explained variance across semantically relevant ROIs. Bars show mean performance across subjects, with individual values overlaid and error bars indicating the standard error. SCRIBEC explains more unique variance than QAEmb on average in all four ROIs, with significant differences in LTC (p = 0.039) and AG (p = 0.023).

Table 3: Overview of the semantic properties from the feature space of Binder et al. (2016), grouped by modality and cognitive domain. Each concept is represented as a vector over these interpretable semantic features. The table lists the 68 properties that are queried individually: the three bipolar properties Temperature, Texture, and Weight of the original 65-dimensional space are each split into their two poles (Hot/Cold, Smooth/Rough, Light/Heavy), and the two resulting scores are recombined by taking their maximum, yielding the final 65 properties (Appendix B.2.1).
Figure 4: Distribution of semantic feature scores derived from human ratings in the Binder et al. (2016) dataset (composed of 535 words), shown for each of the 65 semantic properties.
Table 4: Prompt variants evaluated in the prompt ablation study. Each variant modifies a single component of the base prompt while leaving all other components unchanged.

Table 5: Prompt ablation results across individual models and their ensemble on the 535 words of Binder et al. (2016). Pearson correlation and MSE are computed per word across the 65 properties and averaged over words. The base prompt is the main prompt; its values differ slightly from Table 1 because of non-deterministic GPU inference across runs.
Table 6: Examples of the context provided to SCRIBE for different context window sizes. The target word is shown in bold.

Figure 5: Distribution of (concept, property) pairs across discretized baseline bins under two binning strategies. (a) Quantile-based thresholds (0.34, 1.5) yield more uniform distributions across bins; however, the threshold for the high bin is low relative to the full rating scale (0–6), leading to less interpretable groupings. (b) Manual thresholds aligned with the original rating scale ([0, 2), [2, 4), [4, 6]) produce more interpretable assignments of low, mid, and high association levels across properties. These observations motivate the use of fixed thresholds in our synthetic dataset construction.

Table 7: Examples of controlled contextual manipulations for selected property-concept pairs. For each pair, the low-context sentence is designed to reduce the target semantic property, while the high-context sentence increases it, demonstrating how context systematically modulates semantic feature annotations.
Table 8: Brain regions and corresponding ROI labels.

Figure 6: Distribution of mean squared error (MSE) for out-of-context semantic annotation across models. For each model, we show the distribution of the MSE values computed on the true concept–property assignments (left) and under a permutation baseline obtained by randomly shuffling concept–property pairs (right). Across all models, the true MSE distribution is substantially lower than the permutation baseline, indicating that LLM-based annotations capture meaningful semantic structure beyond chance. Results are shown for individual models and the ensemble.

Figure 7: Distribution of Pearson correlation between LLM-generated semantic annotations and human ratings across models. For each model, we show the distribution of correlation values computed on the true concept–property assignments (left) and under a permutation baseline obtained by randomly shuffling concept–property pairs (right). Across all models, the true correlation distribution is substantially higher than the permutation baseline, indicating that LLM-based annotations capture meaningful semantic structure beyond chance. Results are shown for individual models and the ensemble.
Table 9: Participant flow per data-collection round and questionnaire version. Each version covers half of the concept–property pairs.

Table 10: Contextual modulation of semantic feature scores for the human-evaluated subset. We report mean scores for human judgments and the SCRIBE ensemble across the original (O), lowtarget (LT), and high-target (HT) conditions, together with two- and one-sided Wilcoxon signedrank tests. Results are shown across all concept–property pairs (AllO) and stratified by original out-of-context association strength (LO, MO, HO). Human means are computed from all ratings of each item. For pairs with low baseline association (LO), low-target contexts do not further decrease human ratings, consistent with a floor effect.

Table 11: Comparison of low-target (LT ), original/no-context (O), and high-target (HT ) scores assigned by human annotators, individual LLMs, and LLM ensembles to the evaluated subset of the synthetic dataset. O denotes each annotator’s own out-of-context score. All annotators exhibit the intended ordering LT < O < HT , with significant differences in all three expected directions (LT < O, HT > O, and HT > LT ; all p < .05, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over concept–property pairs). Two-sided tests are also reported for completeness. The ensemble excluding Llama3.1-8B provides a control excluding the model used to generate the synthetic sentences.

Figure 8: Reliability of the mean human rating as a function of the number of raters per item. Lines show the Spearman–Brown prediction from ICC(1, 1) (shaded: ± SD over 20 subsamples). Markers show empirical estimates from random subsets of raters: circles, ICC(1, n) computed on n rater columns; crosses, the correlation between the means of two disjoint groups of n raters (error bars: SD over subsamples). The dotted line marks n = 8, the number of raters used in the main analyses; dashed grey lines mark reliabilities of 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9.

Table 16: Per-model results for the controlled contextual manipulation experiment (see Section 4.2 and Appendix A.3) using all the contextual generated sentences. We report average semantic scores and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for each individual model and their ensemble. O denotes each model’s own out-of-context score. For all models and the ensemble, semantic feature values shift in the intended direction (HT > O > LT) across all pairs and within the mid and high bins. For pairs with low baseline association (LO), llama3.1-8b and mistral-7b do not lower scores further in the low-target condition, mirroring the floor effect observed in human judgments (Table 10); the ensemble shows significant effects in all bins.

Table 17: Brain encoding correlations across context sizes using llama3.1-8b-instruct. We compare out-of-context annotations, fixed-size context windows (k ∈ {3, 5, 10, 50}), and an up to concept condition including all preceding stimulus context. Results are reported for three POS subsets: Nouns, Nouns, Verbs, Adjectives, and All Semantic POS. Values correspond to noise-ceilingnormalized correlations. Bold indicates the best context within each POS group, and underlining indicates the overall best configuration. ∗ denotes significant improvements over the out-of-context baseline (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05).

Figure 10: Unique variance explained by SCRIBEC and QAEmb across cortical regions. Bars show the mean unique explained variance across subjects, with error bars indicating the standard error of the mean; individual dots represent subjects. p-values correspond to one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests testing whether the unique variance explained by SCRIBEC is greater than that explained by QAEmb. Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < 0.05).

Table 21: Noise-ceiling-normalized brain encoding correlations for SCRIBE (SCRIBEC), QAEmb, and their combined representation, evaluated across the whole brain and semantic language ROIs. Values are reported for individual subjects and as mean ± standard error across subjects. ∗ denotes that QAEmb + SCRIBEC significantly outperforms both individual representations (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p < 0.05).

Figure 11: Voxel-wise unique variance explained by SCRIBE and QAEmb across subjects. Variance partitioning was performed directly between the two representations, without including the syntactic control features. Red regions indicate greater unique variance explained by SCRIBE, whereas blue regions indicate greater unique variance explained by QAEmb. Only voxels with a noise ceiling above 0.4 are shown. Across subjects, the maps predominantly show greater unique variance for SCRIBE, particularly in language-related cortical areas, although this pattern is less pronounced in Subject 8.

Table 22: Noise-ceiling-normalized brain encoding correlations for SCRIBEC before and after feature selection, evaluated across the whole brain and semantic language ROIs. Feature selection reduces the representation from 65 to 33 semantic dimensions. Values are reported for individual subjects and as mean ± standard error across subjects. At the whole-brain level, performance does not significantly differ after feature selection (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

Figure 12: Variance partitioning of SCRIBEC and QAEmb with syntactic features across languagerelated ROIs. (a) Brain-predictive variance shared with the syntactic feature space. (b) Unique brain-predictive variance retained by each representation after accounting for the syntactic feature space. Bars show means across subjects and error bars indicate the standard error of the mean. Bold ROI labels and asterisks indicate significant paired differences between SCRIBEC and QAEmb (one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05).

Figure 13: Permutation-based significance testing of the unique neural variance explained by SCRIBEC after accounting for syntactic features. Histograms show permutation-based null distributions, and dashed lines indicate the observed unique variance.

Figure 14: Brain-encoding performance of Llama2-7b, QAEmb, and SCRIBEC . (a) Whole-brain encoding performance. (b) Encoding performance across the Late Language, lateral temporal cortex (LTC), IFG/MFG, and Angular Gyrus ROIs. Bars show mean noise-ceiling-normalized correlation across subjects, individual points represent subjects, and error bars indicate the standard error of the mean. Asterisks indicate significant differences between SCRIBEC and the corresponding baseline (p < 0.05; one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

Figure 15: Shared brain-predictive variance with syntactic features for contextual Llama2-7B and SCRIBE (SCRIBEC). Bars show the mean shared variance across subjects and error bars indicate the standard error of the mean. SCRIBE shares significantly less variance with the syntactic feature space than Llama2-7B in IFG/MFG (one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05), indicated by the bold ROI label and asterisk.

Figure 16: Permutation-based significance testing of the unique neural variance explained by SCRIBEC in variance partitioning with Llama2-7b. Histograms show permutation-based null distributions, and dashed lines indicate the observed unique variance.
